canonical_topic: Volatility Term Structure: Spot Markets Are More Volatile Than Distant Forward Contracts
definition: Nearby (short-dated) futures/forward contracts exhibit higher volatility than contracts further from expiration, because near-term prices are driven by short-term, fast-moving supply and demand shifts, while distant forward prices are shaped mainly by longer-run seasonal expectations.
core_idea: Volatility decreases the further out a contract's expiration is, since near-dated prices reflect immediate, hard-to-predict local conditions while far-dated prices reflect more stable seasonal/macro views.
key_points: The 1st (nearest) contract month is the most volatile, with volatility declining for the 2nd, 3rd, etc. months out, per the source's referenced diagram.
Driver of the effect: spot/near-term prices respond to volatile short-term supply-demand variation; distant forward prices respond to steadier seasonal expectations.
relationships: Forward market mechanics and its volatility-reducing role
Local fragmentation and volatility of spot markets
trading_implications: When assessing price risk, expect nearer-dated positions to carry materially more volatility exposure than longer-dated ones.
